replies.user: How does an LLM actually generate its answers?
replies.raw:
It predicts the next most likely **token** (a word or word-chunk), one at a time, based on patterns learned from massive amounts of text.

There's no lookup table of facts — just billions of weights that shape which token comes next, given everything before it.

So here's the tension: if it's just predicting likely continuations, what's the difference between a model that "knows" something and one that just *sounds* like it does?

replies.user: I think it predicts the next word based on patterns it learned?
replies.raw:
Exactly right — that's the core mechanism.

Now push it one step further: if the model learned those patterns from text written by humans who *do* know things, what could go wrong when it generates text about a topic that wasn't well-represented in its training data?

replies.user: So it doesn't really 'know' facts — it just produces likely text?
replies.raw:
That's the key insight — and it's why fluent output can still be completely false.

A model can generate a confident, well-structured answer about a topic it has almost no reliable signal on, because *sounding right* and *being right* use the same mechanism.

What does that imply about how you should treat any AI-generated claim that you can't immediately verify?

replies.user: Then why does it sometimes state wrong things so confidently?
replies.raw:
Because confidence is a pattern too.

Training data is full of authoritative-sounding text — textbooks, articles, encyclopedias — so the model learned that declarative, confident sentences are *likely* continuations. It has no internal alarm that fires when it's on shaky ground.

What would a responsible workflow look like if you're using an LLM for research?

replies.user: Where does an AI model's knowledge come from?
replies.raw:
It comes from patterns in its **training data** — text (and sometimes images, code, audio) collected before training began.

The model doesn't look things up in real time; it compresses statistical patterns from that data into its weights.

So here's the tension: if the training data ended in, say, early 2025, what happens when you ask the model about something that occurred after that cutoff?

replies.user: From the internet, I guess — so whatever people wrote online.
replies.raw:
Close — that's a big slice, but not the whole picture.

Training data often includes books, academic papers, code repositories, and licensed content alongside web text.

Here's the sharper question though: if the data comes from "whatever people wrote," what does that imply about whose perspectives or facts might be *over-* or *under-represented*?

replies.user: Does that mean gaps in the data become gaps in the model?
replies.raw:
Exactly — and it goes further than gaps.

If certain groups, languages, or viewpoints are *underrepresented*, the model doesn't just "not know" them — it may confidently fill the silence with the majority pattern instead.

What would that look like in practice if you asked a model to describe a "typical doctor"?

replies.user: How would I even notice a gap like that when I use it?
replies.raw:
That's the hard part — you often won't, unless you probe deliberately.

One method: ask the model the same question from multiple angles or perspectives and compare the answers for consistency and whose voice dominates.

What would you look for specifically if you ran that test on the "typical doctor" example?

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a fact that surprises most people: the AI reading your message right now has never seen a single word.

Not one.

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens when you hit send — and it works on chunks, not words.

Your text gets sliced into tokens, which are fragments of text (sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one, sometimes punctuation). Each token maps to a number. "Unbelievable" might become three tokens: "Un", "believ", "able" — each with its own ID in a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 entries.

Here's why this matters: the model never processes letters or words. It processes *lists of numbers*. "I went to the bank" becomes something like [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] before the model touches it.

That sentence is a good example of the problem this creates. Does "bank" mean a riverbank or a financial institution? To you, context makes it obvious.

To the tokenizer, "bank" is just token #3331 — same number either way.

The model has to figure out meaning from the *pattern* of numbers around it, not from understanding the word itself.

[CHECK]If the word "bank" always becomes the same token number regardless of context, how do you think the model figures out which meaning is intended?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and the "same token, different meaning" problem is exactly what the next piece solves.

The model uses something called the **attention mechanism** to figure out which other tokens in the sentence are most relevant to understanding each token.

When the model hits token #3331 ("bank"), it doesn't just look at that token in isolation. It looks at every other token in the sentence and asks: which ones should I weight heavily when interpreting this one?

In "I went to the bank to deposit my paycheck," the tokens "deposit" and "paycheck" pull high attention weight toward "bank." The model learns that *those* tokens are the ones that resolve the ambiguity.

In "I sat by the bank and watched the river," the tokens "river" and "sat" do the same job in the opposite direction.

Same token. Completely different context. Attention is what makes the difference.

This happens across every token simultaneously, in layers — the model runs this process dozens of times, each layer building a richer understanding of how the tokens relate to each other.

[CHECK]In the sentence "The surgeon picked up her scalpel," which token do you think would pull the most attention weight when the model is interpreting "her" — and why?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You've got the right intuition — attention is doing exactly that contextual weighting work.

One small precision worth adding: embeddings aren't just a static map of similar meanings. They're more like a starting point that attention then *reshapes* based on context. The word "bank" starts near its neighbors in embedding space, and then attention updates its representation based on what's around it in *this specific sentence*.

The two ideas work together.

Now for the payoff — what does all this actually *produce*?

After attention has run through its layers, the model does something surprisingly simple: **next-token prediction**.

It looks at all the tokens so far, with all their attention-weighted context, and outputs a probability distribution over every token in its 100,000-token vocabulary.

"The cat sat on the ___" might give "mat" 34% probability, "floor" 18%, "couch" 12%, and so on down the list. The model picks from that distribution — and then the whole process repeats for the *next* token.

Your entire response is generated one token at a time, each prediction feeding into the next.

This is why AI can write fluently but still be wrong — it's optimizing for *what token is likely to come next*, not for *what is true*.

---

Which words do you think the model would predict with **high confidence** as likely next tokens if the sentence stopped mid-way — and which would it struggle with? Now I want your answer to the actual exercise, because it's where this gets interesting.

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant every other word in a sequence is when processing a given word.

So in "The bank by the river flooded," the model learns that "bank" should attend heavily to "river" and "flooded" — not to "money."

What do you think would happen if every word attended equally to every other word, with no weighting at all?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Close — but there's one thing worth sharpening: in a standard transformer, each token attends to **all** tokens in its context window, not just earlier ones (in the encoder, at least).

The decoder is where the "only look back" rule kicks in — to prevent the model from cheating during training by peeking at future tokens.

So what do you think changes about the model's job when it's *generating* new text, versus when it's *reading* a full sentence to understand it?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
Let's go deeper into the *mechanism* underneath attention — how the weighting actually gets computed.

Each token is projected into three vectors: **Query**, **Key**, and **Value**.

- The Query is roughly "what am I looking for?"
- The Key is roughly "what do I advertise about myself?"
- The Value is "what do I actually contribute if selected?"

Attention works by taking a token's Query and computing a dot product against every other token's Key. A high dot product means strong relevance. Those scores get normalized through a softmax — turning them into a probability distribution that sums to 1.

Then the model takes a weighted sum of all the Values using those probabilities.

That weighted sum is what flows forward. The token doesn't "read" other tokens directly — it receives a blend of their Values, weighted by relevance.

---

Now the part most explanations skip: this happens not once, but in **multiple heads simultaneously** — hence *multi-head* attention.

Each head learns a different projection of Q, K, and V. One head might learn syntactic relationships (subject → verb). Another might track coreference ("she" → "Maria"). Another might capture semantic similarity.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back into a single representation.

This is why transformers are so expressive: no single attention pattern has to do all the work.

---

One failure mode worth knowing: attention is **quadratic in sequence length**. Double the tokens, quadruple the computation. This is why long-context models are expensive and why researchers are building alternatives like sparse attention and state-space models.

---

Here's the tension I want you to sit with: the Q/K/V weights are *learned* during training — the model discovers what to attend to, not a human programmer.

What does that imply about whether we can fully explain *why* a model attends to what it does?

Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into ChatGPT, the model doesn't see that word at all.

It sees three chunks: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"**.

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — and tokens aren't words. They're the model's own alphabet, built from patterns in training data.

[EX]GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. A common word like "cat" is one token. A rare word like "photosynthesis" might be two or three. Numbers, punctuation, even spaces get their own tokens.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of number-coded chunks — the only thing the model can actually process.[/KEY]

Here's what makes this interesting: the model doesn't know what a word *means* yet at this stage. It just knows which numbered tokens showed up, in which order. Meaning comes later.

So before we get there — quick check:

[Q]
The word "running" gets split into two tokens: "run" and "ning". What does this tell you about how LLMs read text?
A) They understand grammar rules and split words at meaningful boundaries
B) They split text based on frequency patterns in training data, not meaning
C) They treat every letter as a separate token
ANS: B

replies.user: I picked B) They split text based on frequency patterns in training data, not meaning
replies.raw:
Exactly right — tokenization is purely statistical, not linguistic. The model splits "running" into "run" + "ning" because that pattern compressed the training data efficiently, not because it understands verb stems.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is tokens, the model needs to figure out what each token *means in context* — and that's where **next-token prediction** comes in.

The model's entire job, at its core, is one repeated question: *given everything I've seen so far, what token comes next?*

It does this by assigning a probability to every token in its vocabulary. The highest-probability token wins (usually), gets added to the output, and then the process repeats — one token at a time, left to right, until the response is done.

[EX]Finish this: "The cat sat on the ___". Your brain jumps to "mat" or "floor" — high probability. "The cat sat on the *democracy*" scores near zero. GPT-4 is doing the same math, just across 100,000 options simultaneously.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates responses one token at a time, each chosen by probability — it never "looks up" a pre-written answer.[/KEY]

You ask an LLM "What is the capital of France?" It answers "Paris." How did it arrive at that answer?

When it says "Paris," it's not retrieving a stored fact. It's producing the token that its weights make most likely after seeing "What is the capital of France?"

The distinction matters a lot in practice. A database either has a fact or it doesn't — and it won't make one up. An LLM will always produce *something* plausible, even when it's wrong, because it's optimizing for probability, not truth.

Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it probably doesn't see one word — it sees **three pieces**: "un", "believ", "able."

That's because LLMs don't read words. They read **tokens**.

A token is a chunk of text — sometimes a whole word, sometimes a syllable, sometimes just a punctuation mark. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. Every word you type gets sliced into these chunks, and each chunk gets converted into a number.

So "Hello, world!" might become something like [15496, 11, 995, 0] — just a list of integers the model can do math on.

Here's why this matters: the model has no idea what a "word" is in the human sense. It only ever sees streams of numbers.

[CHECK]If you typed the sentence "I visited the bank" into an LLM, how many separate tokens do you think that might produce — and why might the word "bank" be tricky for the system to handle?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.

Exactly right — and the "bank" example is a perfect illustration of why that matters. The tokenizer has no idea if "bank" means a riverbank or a financial institution. It just assigns it a number and moves on.

The *meaning* has to emerge later.

Which brings us to the next piece: **next-token prediction**.

Here's the core idea: an LLM's entire job, at the most fundamental level, is to answer one question over and over — *"given everything I've seen so far, what token comes next?"*

That's it. No lookup table. No database query.

Just a very sophisticated guess about the most probable next chunk of text.

Take this sentence: "The cat sat on the ___"

The model has seen millions of sentences like this in training. So tokens like "mat", "floor", and "couch" get very high probability scores. Tokens like "democracy" or "17" get scores near zero.

The model picks from that probability distribution — and then does it again for the *next* token, and the next, until it decides to stop.

An entire paragraph of AI output is just this one prediction repeated hundreds of times in a row.

[CHECK]If next-token prediction is just picking the most probable word each time, why might that sometimes produce text that *sounds* fluent and confident but is actually factually wrong?[/CHECK]

Next-token prediction optimizes for **plausibility**, not truth.

The model isn't asking "is this accurate?" It's asking "does this token fit the pattern of text I've seen?" Those two things often overlap — but not always.

If the training data contained a lot of confident-sounding wrong statements, the model learned that confident-sounding text is a good pattern to reproduce. Fluency and accuracy are completely separate properties, and the model only directly trains on one of them.

This is why an LLM can write a fake legal citation in perfect Bluebook format — the *pattern* of a citation is something it learned, even if the underlying case never existed.

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant each word in a sequence is to every other word — before deciding what to output.

So in "The bank by the river flooded," attention helps the model link "bank" to "river" rather than to "money."

What do you think happens to that relevance score when the sentence gets much longer?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Exactly — and it also looks at itself.

The key move: each token generates three vectors (Query, Key, Value). The Query asks "what am I looking for?"

and the Keys from all other tokens answer "here's what I am." The dot product of those two becomes the relevance score.

What do you think the Value vector's job is, once the scores are calculated?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
Once the relevance scores are computed and normalized (via softmax, so they sum to 1), each token collects a **weighted sum of the Value vectors** from every other token.

Think of it this way: the scores decide *how much* to borrow from each token; the Values decide *what* is actually borrowed.

---

So after attention runs, each token's representation is no longer just "what I am" — it's "what I am, reshaped by what I attended to."

That's the deep move: attention doesn't just route information, it *rewrites* each token's meaning in context.

---

Here's where it gets interesting: a single attention pass gives you one "view" of relevance.

But transformers run **multi-head attention** — several attention mechanisms in parallel, each with its own Q/K/V weights.

One head might track syntactic agreement ("the *dogs* that chased the cat *were* fast").

Another might track coreference ("she... *Maria*").

Another might track semantic proximity.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back into a single representation.

---

One failure mode worth knowing: attention is computed between *every* pair of tokens.

That means the compute cost scales as O(n²) with sequence length — double the tokens, quadruple the work.

This is why long-context models are hard and expensive to build, and why researchers have proposed sparse attention, linear attention, and other approximations to escape that quadratic wall.

[SOURCE: Attention Is All You Need — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

---

Given that each head learns its own relevance pattern, what do you think would happen to model quality if you used only one head instead of many?

Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "river bank" and "bank" in "bank account" look identical to you — but an LLM has to figure out which one you mean *before* it can say anything useful back.

That disambiguation problem is exactly where we start.

**Tokenization** is the very first thing that happens when you hit send.

Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words — it gets sliced into *tokens*, which are chunks of text (sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one). Those chunks are then converted into numbers, because math is all a neural network can actually do.

[EX]GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. The word "unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness". A short sentence like "I love AI" could be just four tokens.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into numbered chunks — the model never sees letters or words, only numbers.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as input after tokenization?
A) Your original words, spelled out letter by letter
B) A sequence of numbers representing text chunks
C) A search query sent to the internet
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing text chunks
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model is doing math on numbers the whole time, never reading words the way you do.

Now, those numbers don't just sit in a list. The model needs to understand *relationships* — that "bank" means something different next to "river" than next to "account." That's where the next piece comes in.

**Embeddings and attention** are how the model builds meaning from those numbers.

Each token gets mapped into a point in a massive mathematical space — think of it like a map where similar-meaning words cluster near each other. Then the *attention mechanism* lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide what's relevant.

[EX]In the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired," the attention mechanism figures out that "it" refers to "animal" — not "street." That's not a lookup; it's computed from the relationships between all the tokens simultaneously.[/EX]

[KEY]The attention mechanism lets the model weigh how much each word in your prompt matters to every other word — that's how context shapes meaning.[/KEY]

[Q]
Why does the attention mechanism matter for understanding "I went to the river bank"?
A) It looks up "bank" in a dictionary to find the right definition
B) It searches the internet for context about rivers
C) It weighs the relationship between "bank" and "river" to resolve the ambiguity
ANS: C

There's no dictionary. No lookup table. No database being queried.

The model resolves "bank" by doing math — specifically, by computing how strongly "river" pulls the meaning of "bank" toward *riverbank* rather than *financial institution*. That pull is baked into billions of numerical weights learned during training. It's all arithmetic, happening in parallel across every token in your prompt.

[KEY]Attention is computed, not looked up — the model calculates relationships between tokens using learned numerical weights.[/KEY]

Now you're ready for the final piece: what the model actually *does* with all that context.

**Next-token prediction** is the engine behind every response you've ever gotten from an LLM.

After attention has built up a rich picture of your prompt, the model does one thing: it predicts the single most likely next token. Then it does it again. And again — one token at a time — until the response is complete.

[EX]Given "The cat sat on the ___", the model assigns high probability to "mat", "floor", "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from the high-probability options and keeps going.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates responses by predicting one token at a time — the whole reply is built token by token, not planned in advance.[/KEY]

[Q]
What is an LLM actually doing when it generates a response?
A) Retrieving a pre-written answer from a database
B) Predicting the next most likely token, repeatedly
C) Translating your question into code and running it
ANS: B

Each token gets converted into a number (really, a long list of numbers called a vector). That's the only thing the model ever actually processes — numbers, all the way down.

Here's a concrete example: the sentence "I went to the bank" is genuinely ambiguous. Is it a riverbank or a financial bank? A human uses context to know instantly.

The tokenizer just chops it up and passes the numbers along — figuring out *which* bank comes later, inside the model.

Exactly right — and the detail about word boundaries is the one most people miss. Tokens are about *efficient compression*, not grammar.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those number-lists (vectors) don't just encode *what* a token is — they encode *relationships*.

The model lives in what researchers call an **embedding space**: a giant mathematical landscape where tokens that behave similarly end up close together. "King" and "queen" are near each other. "Bank" (financial) and "bank" (river) actually land in *different neighborhoods* depending on the surrounding tokens — that's how context gets resolved.

The mechanism that does this context-reading is called **attention**. When the model processes "bank" in your sentence, attention lets every token look at every other token and ask: *how much should I care about you right now?* "Went to the" pushes "bank" toward the financial neighborhood.

"Muddy river" would push it the other way.

Real example: in 2017, Google researchers published "Attention Is All You Need" — the paper that introduced this mechanism and launched the entire modern LLM era.
[SOURCE: Attention Is All You Need — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

[CHECK]Here's the key test: "bank" appears in two sentences — "She deposited cash at the bank" and "The kayak tipped near the bank." Same token, same starting vector. What does the attention mechanism do differently for each sentence?[/CHECK]

It picks one (with some randomness built in), appends it, then runs the whole process again with the new token added.

This is why AI sounds fluent but can be wrong — it's optimizing for *what comes next plausibly*, not for *what is true*. A confident-sounding wrong answer and a confident-sounding right answer look identical to the prediction engine.

Real example: ask an LLM to continue "The capital of Australia is..." and it'll say "Canberra" easily. Ask something obscure and it'll still produce a high-confidence-sounding token — whether or not it's accurate.

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant each word in a sequence is to every other word — not just its neighbors.

So in "The bank by the river flooded," attention helps the model connect "bank" to "river" and "flooded" rather than treating all nearby words equally.

Why do you think that matters more for language than, say, a simple left-to-right reading order?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Mostly right — but "looks back" undersells it.

In the full attention mechanism, every token attends to **every other token simultaneously**, including ones that come after it (during training, at least).

What do you think would break if a token could only ever look backward and never forward?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
Let's go deeper into the machinery itself.

Each token gets turned into three vectors: a **Query**, a Key, and a Value.

Think of it like a search engine inside the model: the Query is what a token is "asking for," the Keys are what every other token is "advertising," and the Values are what gets actually retrieved if the match is strong.

The attention score between two tokens is computed by taking the dot product of one token's Query with another token's Key — a high dot product means "these two are relevant to each other." Those scores get normalized with a softmax so they sum to 1, becoming weights. Then the model takes a weighted sum of all the Value vectors using those weights.

That weighted sum is what the token "receives" from attending to the sequence.

---

Now here's where it gets interesting: transformers don't run this once.

They run **multi-head attention** — the same mechanism in parallel, multiple times, with different learned Query/Key/Value weight matrices each time.

Each head learns to attend to something different. One head might track syntactic agreement ("the verb matches its subject"). Another might track coreference ("the pronoun refers to this noun").

Another might track semantic similarity. The outputs of all heads get concatenated and projected back down.

No one programs those specializations — they emerge from training.

---

One honest caveat: interpretability research (like Anthropic's mechanistic interpretability work) is still unpacking what individual heads actually learn. The "one head = one linguistic function" story is a useful intuition, not a settled fact.

[SOURCE: Attention Is All You Need — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

---

That's actually the most common misconception about LLMs — so it's worth pausing here.

A search engine like Google *does* look things up — it finds real pages that already exist and retrieves them.

An LLM does something completely different: it **generates** text from scratch, token by token, based on statistical patterns it learned during training.

There's no database of answers being queried. No index being searched. Just a probability calculation: *given these tokens so far, what comes next?*

Think of it this way: when you autocomplete a text message, your phone isn't looking up what you meant to say. It's predicting what word fits. LLMs do that same thing, but with vastly more sophistication and at much greater length.

[EX]When you ask ChatGPT "What is the capital of France?" it doesn't retrieve a stored fact. It generates tokens that, based on training patterns, are statistically likely to follow that question — and "Paris" happens to be the overwhelmingly likely next token. It gets it right, but not by looking it up.[/EX]

The reason this matters: a search engine *fails* by saying "no results." An LLM *fails* by confidently generating a plausible-but-wrong answer — because plausible is all it's optimizing for.

[Q]
What is an LLM actually doing when it generates a response?
A) Looking up answers in a database
B) Predicting the most likely next token, one at a time
C) Translating your question into search queries
ANS: B
